title: The handbook for the road
hook: Arrian, Epictetus' student, boiled his teacher down into a little book meant to be kept at hand

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rumi's reed, at the big lookout, the top of year one. Your line was look how far. Did you tell someone you'd finished a whole year? Day three hundred thirty-two. Year two begins.

Most books that change lives are too heavy to carry. This one fits in a coat pocket. Around fifty short sections. You can read it on a bus ride and spend the rest of your life on it. Nearly two thousand years ago, in a school on the western coast of Greece, a young man named Arrian sat writing down everything his teacher said. The teacher was an old man with a lame leg who had grown up enslaved, and he never wrote a word himself. The student wrote it all, then boiled it down. Year two opens on the porch. Today: the handbook for the road.
screen: `A BOOK THAT FITS IN A POCKET.` → `A STUDENT TAKING NOTES.` → `THE HANDBOOK FOR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. Epictetus was born around the year fifty in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and grew up enslaved. His owner, Epaphroditus, was a freedman who served at the court of Nero. Somehow the young man was allowed to study with Musonius Rufus, the Stoic we met in year one, the one who called plain food training. Later he was freed and taught philosophy in Rome, until the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from the city near the end of the first century. Epictetus moved to Nicopolis in Greece and opened a school. Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. Second, the student. Arrian, who went on to become a Roman governor and the historian of Alexander the Great, took down his teacher's talks. Those notes became the Discourses; four books survive. Then Arrian made something smaller: the best of it in short, plain sections. Third, the word. Enchiridion is Greek: en, in, and cheir, the hand. Something kept in the hand. The same word could mean a hand-knife, a small blade you keep close. Not a book for the shelf. A tool for the road. People have carried it ever since. Marcus Aurelius thanks one of his teachers for lending him a copy of Epictetus' notes. Christian monks later adapted the handbook for life in their communities. Fourth, the plan. This year we read the Stoics properly and in order: the handbook first, a section or two a day, then the Discourses, Seneca's letters, the whole of Marcus. They're one school among many, and we'll read them on their own terms.
screen: `EPICTETUS: ENSLAVED, FREED, A TEACHER.` · `ARRIAN TAKES THE NOTES.` · `ENCHIRIDION: KEPT IN THE HAND.` · `A YEAR ON THE PORCH, IN ORDER.` · then, large: `KEEP IT AT HAND.`

segments.voice: Find a scrap of paper, or the notes on your phone. Write one line from year one that you want close. Maybe breathe. Maybe look how far. Maybe a line that has stayed with you all year. Fold the paper small and put it in a pocket, a wallet, behind your phone case. Now rest your hand where the note is. Feel how small it is, and how near. Breathe, and let the line sit there under your hand. The bell holds the time.
Enchiridion. Greek for something kept in the hand: Epictetus' teaching, boiled down by his student Arrian, small enough to carry. Today's word.
Your line: keep it at hand. Carry your note all day. When the day gets loud, touch it once, and read it. Day three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism keep a copy of Epictetus' Handbook nearby, or copy a single line onto a card, and reread it during the day.

pairs: the student who took the notes

myth: he wrote nothing; his student Arrian wrote down his teaching and boiled it down.
he was enslaved as a young man and later freed, then taught in Rome and Nicopolis.
enchiridion means a book for the library shelf
it means something kept in the hand; the word could also mean a hand-knife.

fork.setup: you're Arrian. your teacher's talks fill notebooks, and people want something they can carry. what do you make?
options: a little book of the best of it, kept in the hand.
nothing: tell them to come to class.
fork.reveal: Arrian kept the long Discourses and also made the short Handbook, plain sections meant to be carried, not shelved.

original.note: Greek, from en, in, and cheir, hand: something kept in the hand.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fancy word for a manual.
what it means: a small book of Epictetus' teaching, made to be kept in the hand.
what a scholar hears: Arrian also preserved the longer Discourses, of which four books survive, and later wrote the history of Alexander.

sources.ref: Discourses, Arrian's letter to Lucius Gellius

notes: Epictetus' dates (c. 50 – c. 135), birthplace Hierapolis in Phrygia, and his owner Epaphroditus as a freedman at Nero's court: standard accounts; confirm.
Domitian's expulsion of philosophers from Rome: dated variously to 89 or 93–95; the script says only 'near the end of the first century'.
Arrian as the compiler of the Enchiridion is attested by Simplicius' commentary; confirm. Four of the Discourses' books survive (Photius mentions eight).
ἐγχειρίδιον can mean 'hand-knife, dagger' as well as 'handbook' (LSJ); confirm.
Meditations 1.7: Marcus thanks Rusticus for sharing his copy of Epictetus' notes ('hypomnemata'); paraphrased.
Christian monastic adaptations of the Enchiridion (e.g. the paraphrase attributed to Nilus): confirm the phrasing 'adapted the handbook for life in their communities'.
Musonius Rufus as Epictetus' teacher: links to year one, day 299 ('plain food, Musonius's training'). Year two open; camp open.
